Can AI See What Cardiologists Can't?

Using deep learning to find signs of prior heart attack in the cheapest possible ECG signal.

Paper: This demo is a replication of Wang, Schubert & Obermeyer et al. (2026), "AI-Enhanced Handheld ECGs to Screen for Prior Myocardial Infarction in Rural India" (NBER Working Paper 34690). Obermeyer et al. show that a deep learning model reading only a single ECG lead can stratify patients by MI risk, flagging the highest-risk individuals for follow-up imaging, even from a signal that human cardiologists consider diagnostically blind to inferior infarction.

Model: The original paper uses a 1D ResNet-18. We replicate that baseline, then compare seven architectures under identical training conditions. Our CNN-Transformer hybrid (131K parameters, 0.63 MB FP32) achieves the best trade-off between AUC, model size, and inference latency. Pre-trained on the PTB-XL dataset (21,799 ECGs, Germany) to learn general MI features from 12-lead recordings, then fine-tuned on the Ningbo + Shaoxing 12-lead ECG database (Zheng et al. 2020; 45,152 ECGs from Ningbo First Hospital and Shaoxing People's Hospital, China) using only Lead I. This cross-population transfer (training in Europe, deploying in Asia) mirrors the real-world screening scenario Obermeyer et al. envision. Test-set AUC: 0.81 (held-out 40/20/40 split, n=18,062).

Quantization & on-device profiling: The model was exported to ONNX and profiled on real smartphones via Qualcomm AI Hub, targeting the deployment scenario of low-cost handheld ECGs in resource-limited settings. INT8 quantization reduces model size from 0.63 MB to 0.19 MB with no AUC loss (0.855 in both cases), but FP32 is actually faster on-device because the model is already so small that quantization overhead dominates. On a Samsung Galaxy S24 (flagship): 152 µs inference. On a Xiaomi Redmi Note 10 5G (~$100, representative of LMIC devices): 1.96 ms. Deployment recommendation: ship FP32.

Demo data: All 349 ECG recordings in this demo are drawn from the Ningbo + Shaoxing 12-lead ECG database (Zheng et al. 2020). Specifically, they come from the held-out 40/20/40 test split (18,062 records, 49 with inferior MI), which was not used during training or fine-tuning. The demo sample is deliberately enriched for illustration: all 49 MI cases plus 300 randomly sampled non-MI cases are included, so the apparent MI rate here (~14.0%) does not reflect any real-world prevalence.

Note on prevalence: In the full Ningbo + Shaoxing dataset, inferior MI accounts for 0.27% of records (123 out of 45,152). This rate is specific to that dataset and reflects hospital ECG referral traffic: patients who already had symptoms or clinical suspicion warranting an ECG, not the general population. By contrast, China's national cardiovascular surveillance estimates the population-level incidence of acute MI among adults at approximately 88 per 100,000 (0.088%) (JACC, 2025). The model outputs a risk score and percentile rank rather than a binary diagnosis. Enrichment ratios below are reported against both the Shaoxing dataset rate (0.27%) and the population rate (0.088%).

Architecture Comparison

Seven architectures tested under identical training conditions (focal loss, augmentation, full data). Fine-tuned AUC evaluated on the Ningbo+Shaoxing cross-population set used in the architecture sweep (60% split, 27,092 records). Separate from the final 40/20/40 held-out evaluation reported above.

Comparison with Obermeyer et al.

Our replication uses proxy datasets (PTB-XL, Shaoxing) in place of the original Swedish and Tamil Nadu cohorts. Despite smaller pre-training data, the model achieves comparable or better performance.

The Deployment Case

Our CNN-Transformer model runs in under 2ms on a budget smartphone (Xiaomi Redmi Note 10 5G, ~$100). Combined with a handheld ECG device, this enables cardiac risk screening in settings without access to echocardiography — exactly the scenario Obermeyer et al. envision for low- and middle-income countries. Patients in the highest risk tier would be referred for confirmatory imaging, converting a $30,000 echo machine into a $50 handheld screen.
